props.title: The Art of the Steal

sections.content: The Art of the Steal stands as one of documentary cinema's most gripping examinations of art world politics and cultural preservation. Director Don Argott meticulously unravels the controversial fate of the Barnes Foundation's $25 billion art collection, turning what could've been dry institutional politics into a thrilling investigation of power, money, and betrayal. The film's approach echoes the investigative intensity of Inside Job (2010) and Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room (2005), while maintaining the artistic focus of Exit Through the Gift Shop (2010).

sections.content: The documentary exists within a rich tradition of films exposing art world machinations. Herb & Dorothy (2008) provides a contrasting view of art collecting through the story of the Vogels, postal workers who amassed one of the most important contemporary art collections in history. Meanwhile, Beltracchi: The Art of Forgery (2014) delves into the dark side of art authentication and market manipulation, complementing the institutional corruption exposed in The Art of the Steal. SUBHEAD: The Politics of Cultural Heritage

The film's exploration of cultural heritage preservation connects to broader documentary investigations of institutional power. Like Citizen Koch (2013) and Dark Money (2018), it reveals how wealthy interests can reshape public institutions. The Barnes controversy particularly resonates with The New Rijksmuseum (2014), which chronicles another museum's transformation, though with vastly different motivations and outcomes.
